directions: Question 1 (Document-Based Question). Suggested time: 60 minutes (about 15 minutes reading and planning, about 45 minutes writing). This question is based on the 7 documents that follow. In your response you should: respond with a historically defensible thesis that establishes a line of reasoning; describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt; use the content of at least 6 documents to support your argument; include at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents; for at least 2 documents, explain how the document's historical situation, intended audience, purpose, or point of view is relevant to your argument; and demonstrate a complex understanding of the topic, for example by corroborating, qualifying, or modifying your argument.

documents.source: Cartoon map illustrating General Winfield Scott's 'Anaconda Plan,' by J. B. Elliott, 1861 (public domain)
documents.text: [Image description] A satirical 1861 map of the eastern United States shows a giant snake — the Union blockade — coiling around the Confederacy's coastline, while a second snake winds down the Mississippi River, squeezing the South from the sea and splitting it along the great river. The cartoon visualizes the Union strategy: strangle Southern trade with a naval blockade and seize the Mississippi to divide the Confederacy.

documents.source: Map of Confederate territory losses, 1861–1865, Office of the Chief of Military History, United States Army (public domain, U.S. federal government work)
documents.text: [Image description] A series of shaded maps shows Confederate-held territory shrinking year by year: in 1861 the Confederacy controls nearly the entire South; by 1863 Union advances have split it at the Mississippi and taken Tennessee and much of the Atlantic coast; by 1865 only small pockets around Richmond and the Deep South interior remain under Confederate control.

documents.source: J. M. Edmunds, Commissioner of the General Land Office, 'Manufactures of the United States in 1860: Compiled from the Original Returns of the Eighth Census,' published 1865 (public domain)
documents.text: "Without our manufacturing capacities whence could we have drawn the materials of war? ... It was manufacturing and mechanical resources and the granaries of the West which enabled the republic to arm, subsist, and pay immense armies, and create iron-clad fleets to meet the emergency. It was mainly for the want of these, and not for lack of courage, will, or skill, that the revolt failed."

documents.source: Comparative resources of the Union and the Confederacy in 1861, adapted from 1860 census data (factual data; original presentation)
documents.text: Population: Union led 2.5 to 1. Free men of military age: Union led 4.4 to 1. Value of factory production: Union led 10 to 1. Railroad mileage: Union led 2.4 to 1. Iron production: Union led 20 to 1. Coal production: Union led 38 to 1. Firearms production: Union led 32 to 1. Naval ship tonnage: Union led 25 to 1. Wheat production: Union led 4.2 to 1. Cotton production: Confederacy led 24 to 1.

documents.source: General William Tecumseh Sherman, letter to Professor David F. Boyd, December 24, 1860 (public domain)
documents.text: "You people of the South don't know what you are doing... The North can make a steam engine, locomotive, or railway car; hardly a yard of cloth or pair of shoes can you make. You are rushing into war with one of the most powerful, ingeniously mechanical, and determined people on Earth — right at your doors... In all else you are totally unprepared... If your people will but stop and think, they must see in the end that you will surely fail."

documents.source: General William T. Sherman, Special Field Orders No. 120, November 9, 1864 (public domain; paraphrased)
documents.text: [Paraphrased] Sherman orders his army, marching through Georgia, to forage liberally off the countryside for food and supplies, and authorizes corps commanders to destroy mills, houses, cotton gins, and railroads in hostile districts. The orders aim to strip the Confederacy of the economic resources sustaining its armies.

documents.source: President Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862 (public domain)
documents.text: "If I could save the Union without freeing any slave I would do it, and if I could save it by freeing all the slaves I would do it; and if I could save it by freeing some and leaving others alone I would also do that."

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which industrialization caused the Union to succeed over the Confederacy during the Civil War.

rubric_map.analysis_and_reasoning_2_points: Sourcing (1 pt): explain the relevance of historical situation, audience, purpose, or point of view for at least 2 documents — e.g., Edmunds (Doc 3) writes as a federal official justifying the Union war effort after victory, so his claim that industry decided the war serves a vindicating purpose; Sherman (Doc 5) writes privately in 1860 to a Southern friend as a warning, not propaganda, which strengthens his testimony about Northern industrial advantage. Complexity (1 pt): demonstrate a complex understanding — e.g., qualify the argument by showing industrialization was necessary but not sufficient (it required Lincoln's political leadership, emancipation as a war measure, and military strategy to convert material advantage into victory), or corroborate across multiple document types (statistics, strategy maps, and personal testimony all pointing the same way).
rubric_map.contextualization_1_point: Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Market Revolution's creation of a Northern industrial economy and a Southern slave-based staple economy before the war, or the Emancipation Proclamation's transformation of the war into a fight against slavery that blocked European intervention.
rubric_map.evidence_3_points: Describe the content of at least 3 documents (1 pt); use the content of at least 6 documents to support the argument (1 pt); include at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents (1 pt) — e.g., the Union's ironclad warships, the Homestead Act and Pacific Railway Act expanding Northern economic power during the war, or the Confederacy's inability to replace railroad iron as its network decayed.
rubric_map.thesis_1_point: Respond with a historically defensible thesis that establishes a line of reasoning, e.g.: 'Industrialization was the decisive cause of Union victory because it gave the North the weapons, transportation, and naval power to sustain a long war and strangle the Southern economy, although converting that material edge into victory still required effective political and military leadership.'
